opus-5.5.text:
I think the main thing would be if we saw the scaling of compute start to stall out well before we get systems that can do most economically valuable work. A lot of my view that AGI could come relatively soon rests on the idea that compute has been growing extremely fast, something like four or five times per year for frontier training runs, and that this growth has been translating into capabilities in a fairly reliable way. If that growth slows down substantially, because we hit limits on chip manufacturing, energy, or simply the willingness of investors to keep pouring tens or hundreds of billions of dollars into training runs, then the timeline stretches out a lot.

So one piece of evidence would be the economic returns. Right now companies are investing heavily on the expectation that these systems will generate enormous revenue. If over the next few years we see AI revenues plateau, if the systems turn out to be useful for some narrow tasks like coding assistance or customer service but they don't really generalize to the broad range of things humans do in the economy, then I think the investment would dry up. Once you stop scaling compute at this rate, you're relying on algorithmic progress and hardware efficiency improvements, which are real but much slower. That world could plausibly push AGI out by decades.

The second thing would be evidence that there are capabilities that just don't come with scale. I've argued before that things like agency, long-horizon planning, and the kind of sensorimotor and common sense competence that's very cheap for humans have been harder than people expected. That's Moravec's paradox, basically. If we keep scaling and these systems remain impressive on benchmarks but brittle when you actually ask them to carry out a multi-week project autonomously, or operate in the physical world, that would update me toward thinking we're missing something fundamental, and that finding it might require research breakthroughs we can't schedule.

And the third would be something like the training data or environment bottleneck. If it turns out that to get these more agentic capabilities you need rich interactive environments or very expensive real-world data, and that's much harder to produce than scraping the internet was, that could slow things down a lot.

I'd say 2100 is not my median, I think it's quite a bit earlier than that, but I don't think it's crazy. If compute scaling stalls around the end of this decade and we haven't crossed the threshold by then, the probability per year drops considerably, and you end up with a pretty long tail.

r001.rationale: The response says that if compute scaling stalls and scaled systems remain brittle or fail to generalize, expectations would shift toward a much longer timeline, making 2100 plausible.

fable-5.1.text:
So, the first thing I'd say is that my own median is actually earlier than 2100, probably somewhere in the 2040s or so. But if you ask what would push me out toward the end of the century, I think it comes down to a few things.

The big one is compute. Right now, the main driver of progress in AI is that we're scaling up training compute by something like four or five times per year, and that's been going on for over a decade. That rate is not sustainable indefinitely. At some point you run into the limits of how much the world is willing to spend on this, how fast you can build fabs and data centers and power plants, and how much further hardware efficiency can improve. If I saw that scaling slow down to, say, the historical trend of Moore's law, so maybe 1.3 to 1.5 times per year, and at the same time the systems we have at that point are still clearly not capable of automating most economically valuable work, then I'd update a lot. Because then you're relying on algorithmic progress alone, and historically that's been substantial but it's also been partly driven by having more compute to run experiments with. So those two things slow down together.

The second thing is if the current paradigm turns out to have some fundamental ceiling. One of the things that makes me somewhat skeptical of very short timelines is that the current models are impressive on benchmarks but they still have a hard time with things like long-horizon agency, learning on the job the way a human employee does, operating in messy real-world environments. If we keep scaling and those problems don't go away, if it looks like you need some qualitatively different approach that nobody has a clear idea for, then you're back in the regime of waiting for conceptual breakthroughs. And conceptual breakthroughs are much harder to forecast. You could wait decades.

And then the third thing is just economic. If AI deployment stalls, if revenue doesn't keep up with the investment, you could see a funding pullback like what happened in previous AI winters, and that would slow everything down. I think that's less likely because the current systems are actually useful, but it's not impossible.

So I guess the short version is: compute scaling hitting a wall before the systems are good enough, combined with no clear path forward algorithmically. If both of those happened, 2100 would start to look quite plausible to me. I just don't think it's the most likely outcome right now.

r001.rationale: The response says expectations would shift toward 2100 if compute scaling slowed before systems could automate most valuable work, and continued scaling failed to resolve key capability problems.

astra-6.text:
I think you’d need evidence that there are important obstacles to AGI that we’re not going to overcome simply by scaling up existing methods. A few disappointing model releases wouldn’t be enough. That could reflect a temporary bottleneck in compute, data, or how effectively we’re using them.

What would move me more is a sustained pattern where we put substantially more resources into these systems and they still fail at the same kinds of tasks. In particular, if systems keep improving on benchmarks but don’t get much better at learning unfamiliar tasks or carrying out complicated projects reliably, that would suggest we’re missing something important.

But there’s a further step from that to 2100. Even if current approaches hit a wall, we have decades to develop new ones. So I’d also need evidence that the missing pieces are very difficult to discover, or that progress in AI research is going to slow down dramatically. Evidence against short timelines isn’t automatically evidence for timelines that long.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that a sustained pattern of adding substantially more resources while systems continue to fail at the same kinds of tasks would suggest current approaches are hitting an important obstacle—evidence that would shift expectations toward a much later arrival.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’d need to see evidence that there are important ingredients missing from our current approaches, and that those ingredients are going to be very difficult to discover. It wouldn’t be enough to see scaling slow down for a couple of years. That could be a temporary bottleneck, or it could mean we need a different approach.

More persuasive evidence would be that we keep increasing compute, improving the data, and putting substantial research effort into these systems, but they still fail at some fairly fundamental capabilities—and we develop a good explanation for why those failures are hard to overcome.

Even then, 2100 is a very long way away. You’re making a claim about what many decades of scientific progress won’t accomplish. So I’d find it easier to update toward longer timelines than to become confident specifically that AGI won’t arrive until the end of the century.

r001.rationale: The response says a couple of years of scaling slowdown would not be enough and instead points to persistent failures despite greater compute, better data, and research effort. It does not identify a prolonged period of scaling working poorly as evidence for AGI arriving around 2100.
